/api/labs.label: Foundations
/api/labs.tagline: Tabular methods on small, fully observable worlds
/api/labs.description: Gridworlds, chains, bandits and textbook MDPs where every state can be counted. Learning is fast enough to watch value estimates spread, which makes this the place to build intuition about exploration, bootstrapping and the discount factor.

curriculum.title: Measure the floor
curriculum.why: A random policy shows what zero skill looks like on this task.

curriculum.title: Watch values propagate
curriculum.why: Episode length should collapse from ~50 steps to the optimal 10.

curriculum.title: On-policy caution
curriculum.why: SARSA learns the safe path away from the cliff edge.

curriculum.title: Off-policy optimism
curriculum.why: Q-learning learns the risky edge path; compare it with SARSA.

curriculum.title: Plan with a model
curriculum.why: Dyna-Q solves the maze in far fewer real episodes than Q-learning.

curriculum.title: Explore with confidence
curriculum.why: Count-based bonuses beat epsilon-greedy without any tuning.

/api/labs.label: Classic Control
/api/labs.description: CartPole, MountainCar, Acrobot, Pendulum and friends. States are a handful of continuous numbers, so neural networks replace tables. This is where deep RL algorithms are compared, debugged and tuned before they scale up.

curriculum.title: Solve CartPole with DQN
curriculum.why: The canonical first deep-RL result: mean return climbs to 500.

curriculum.title: Pure policy gradient
curriculum.why: No value function, high variance. Notice how noisy the curve is.

curriculum.title: Stabilise with PPO
curriculum.why: Clipped updates and a critic make learning steady across seeds.

curriculum.title: Sparse reward
curriculum.why: Nothing happens for a long time, then momentum is discovered.

curriculum.title: First continuous action
curriculum.why: Torque instead of buttons: a stepping stone to MuJoCo.

/api/labs.label: Continuous Control
/api/labs.description: MuJoCo locomotion and manipulation plus Box2D walkers. Actions are vectors of joint torques, observations are dozens of joint angles and velocities, and only off-policy actor-critic methods learn in a reasonable number of samples on a CPU.

curriculum.title: Check the pipeline
curriculum.why: The easiest MuJoCo task. If SAC fails here, something is broken.

curriculum.title: Reach a target
curriculum.why: Two joints, dense reward, a quick manipulation result.

curriculum.title: Learn to run
curriculum.why: No falling over, so the curve rises smoothly with experience.

curriculum.title: Balance and hop
curriculum.why: Early termination on falling makes the curve much noisier.

/api/labs.label: Perception
/api/labs.description: MinAtar re-implements five Atari games on a 10x10 grid of binary feature channels: Atari's difficulty at a fraction of the compute. Observations are images, so representation learning is part of the problem.

curriculum.title: Baseline the game
curriculum.why: Random play on Freeway scores almost nothing.

curriculum.title: DQN on Freeway
curriculum.why: Freeway's dense progress signal makes early learning visible.

curriculum.title: Prioritised replay
curriculum.why: Rare brick-hits get replayed more often than empty frames.

/api/labs.label: Multi-Agent
/api/labs.description: Turn-based board and card games from PettingZoo. The learner plays one seat against a scripted opponent, so reward is win, draw or loss and action masks rule out illegal moves.

curriculum.title: Random vs random
curriculum.why: The first player wins more often even with no skill.

curriculum.title: Never lose
curriculum.why: With masks, DQN learns to block and fork against a random opponent.

curriculum.title: Longer horizons
curriculum.why: Connect Four needs planning several moves ahead.

/api/labs.label: Language models
/api/labs.tagline: RL fine-tuning of a tiny language model
/api/labs.description: The techniques behind reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1, at a scale that runs on a laptop: a small pretrained transformer, tasks with verifiable rewards, and the algorithms that fine-tune it: REINFORCE, GRPO and DPO, with supervised fine-tuning as the baseline. A hackable reward shows why the KL penalty exists.

curriculum.title: The supervised baseline
curriculum.why: Fine-tuning on correct answers: what RL has to beat, and needs labels.

curriculum.title: Learn from a verifier
curriculum.why: GRPO raises sampled accuracy with only a right/wrong signal.

curriculum.title: One baseline for all
curriculum.why: REINFORCE uses one batch-mean baseline; compare its noise with GRPO.

curriculum.title: Learn from preferences
curriculum.why: DPO improves from pairs of answers, with no reward in the loss.

curriculum.title: Reward hacking
curriculum.why: A flawed reward model pays for length; watch reward and accuracy part ways.

/api/envs.name: catch
/api/envs.label: Catch
/api/envs.description: Catch falling items by moving a paddle. A minimal arcade task that exercises delayed credit assignment without pixel complexity.
/api/envs.reward_desc: +1 catch, −1 miss, 0 otherwise.
/api/envs.termination_desc: Item lands (caught or missed) or 100 steps elapsed.

/api/envs.name: dyna_maze
/api/envs.label: Dyna Maze
/api/envs.description: Sutton & Barto's 6x9 maze with three walls and a single reward at the goal. Built to show how much planning with a learned model speeds up a tabular learner.
/api/envs.reward_desc: +1 on reaching the goal, 0 everywhere else.
/api/envs.termination_desc: Goal reached, or truncation at 1000 steps.

/api/envs.name: gridworld
/api/envs.label: Gridworld
/api/envs.description: 6×6 grid navigation: start top-left, reach the goal bottom-right. One-hot state observations make this the perfect first task for tabular methods.
/api/envs.reward_desc: +1 on reaching the goal, −0.01 per step (encourages short paths).
/api/envs.termination_desc: Goal reached or 200 steps elapsed.

/api/envs.name: multi_armed_bandit
/api/envs.label: Multi-Armed Bandit
/api/envs.description: k arms, one state, Gaussian rewards. No generalisation is possible - every bit of performance must come from how well the agent balances trying new arms against exploiting the best one found so far.
/api/envs.reward_desc: Sampled from N(q_a, 1) where q_a is the true value of the chosen arm.
/api/envs.termination_desc: One pull per episode (the horizon is configurable).

/api/envs.name: n_chain
/api/envs.label: N-Chain
/api/envs.description: Walk a chain of states. Bailing out pays a small reward immediately; staying the course pays much more but only at the end of the chain. A clean test of long-horizon credit assignment.
/api/envs.reward_desc: +2 for jumping back to the start; +10 for advancing while at the final state; 0 otherwise.
/api/envs.termination_desc: No terminal state - episodes truncate at 100 steps.

/api/envs.name: nonstationary_bandit
/api/envs.label: Drifting Bandit
/api/envs.description: A 10-armed bandit whose true arm values take a small random walk after every pull. Whatever was best a while ago may not be best now, so exploration can never stop.
/api/envs.reward_desc: Sampled from N(q_a, 1); every q_a drifts by N(0, 0.01) per pull.
/api/envs.termination_desc: One pull per episode.

/api/envs.name: river_swim
/api/envs.label: RiverSwim
/api/envs.description: Swim upstream against a current. Hugging the near bank pays a tiny guaranteed reward; the far bank pays 1.0 per step but is hard to reach. The standard benchmark for showing that naive epsilon-greedy exploration is not enough.
/api/envs.reward_desc: 0.005 for swimming left from the start state; 1.0 for swimming right at the far bank; 0 otherwise.
/api/envs.termination_desc: No terminal state - episodes truncate at 100 steps.

/api/envs.name: windy_gridworld
/api/envs.label: Windy Gridworld
/api/envs.description: Sutton & Barto's gridworld with an updraft that varies by column. Every move is displaced upward by the wind, so reaching the goal requires deliberately overshooting and letting the wind carry you in.
/api/envs.reward_desc: -1 per step until the goal is reached (undiscounted).
/api/envs.termination_desc: Reaching the goal cell, or truncation at 200 steps.

/api/envs.name: blackjack
/api/envs.label: Blackjack-v1
/api/envs.description: Play Blackjack against a fixed dealer policy. The observation is a tuple (player sum, dealer showing card, usable ace) rather than a vector, which makes it a useful test of observation handling.
/api/envs.reward_desc: +1 win, -1 loss, 0 draw (with the optional natural bonus).
/api/envs.termination_desc: Single decision per episode: stick or hit until bust.

/api/envs.name: cliff_walking
/api/envs.label: CliffWalking-v0
/api/envs.description: Walk from start to goal along a cliff edge. The shortest path hugs the cliff and is dangerous; the safe path is much longer. Classic Sutton & Barto example contrasting SARSA and Q-learning.
/api/envs.reward_desc: -1 per step; -100 for stepping off the cliff (which also sends the agent back to the start).
/api/envs.termination_desc: Reaching the goal. Falling off resets to the start rather than ending the episode.

/api/envs.name: frozen_lake
/api/envs.label: FrozenLake-v1
/api/envs.description: Cross a frozen lake from start to goal without falling through a hole. The ice is slippery, so each move only sometimes goes where you intended - the canonical demonstration of why stochastic environments need more than greedy value iteration.
/api/envs.reward_desc: +1 for reaching the goal, 0 otherwise.
/api/envs.termination_desc: Reaching the goal, falling into a hole, or 100 steps.

/api/envs.name: taxi
/api/envs.label: Taxi-v3
/api/envs.description: Drive a taxi: pick up a passenger at one of four locations and drop them at another, navigating walls in a 5x5 grid. The first environment where the state is genuinely composed of several facts (taxi position, passenger location, destination).
/api/envs.reward_desc: +20 for a successful drop-off, -1 per step, -10 for an illegal pick-up or drop-off.
/api/envs.termination_desc: Successful drop-off or 200 steps.

/api/envs.name: acrobot
/api/envs.label: Acrobot-v1
/api/envs.description: Swing up a two-link pendulum by actuating the elbow. Sparse reward, requires energy pumping — a classic underactuated control benchmark.
/api/envs.termination_desc: Tip above threshold or 500 steps.

/api/envs.name: bipedal_walker
/api/envs.label: BipedalWalker-v3
/api/envs.description: Make a bipedal robot walk by actuating 4 joints (Box2D). High-dimensional continuous control, tests sample efficiency and stability.
/api/envs.termination_desc: Fall, 1600 steps, or out of bounds.
/api/envs.unavailable_reason: Requires Box2D, which is not installed. Install with: pip install "gymnasium[box2d]"

/api/envs.name: cartpole
/api/envs.label: CartPole-v1
/api/envs.description: Balance a pole on a moving cart. The canonical RL starter task: dense rewards, tiny state, fast episodes.
/api/envs.termination_desc: Pole falls >12°, cart leaves the track, or 500 steps reached.
limitations: Fully observable; no partial observability challenges.
/api/envs.beginner_exercise: Train DQN with default settings for 300-400 episodes. Watch the mean100 curve climb toward 500 - that is 'solved'.
/api/envs.advanced_exercise: Compare DQN vs PPO over 5 seeds each. Which is more stable? Measure wall-clock time to reach mean100 ≥ 475.

/api/envs.name: lunar_lander
/api/envs.label: LunarLander-v2
/api/envs.description: Land a lunar module softly between two flags using side thrusters and a main engine (Box2D physics).
/api/envs.termination_desc: Crash, successful landing, or 1000 steps.
/api/envs.unavailable_reason: Requires Box2D, which is not installed. Install with: pip install "gymnasium[box2d]"

/api/envs.name: mountain_car
/api/envs.label: MountainCar-v0
/api/envs.description: Drive an underpowered car up a steep hill. The car cannot climb directly - it must build momentum by rocking, which requires long-horizon planning.
/api/envs.termination_desc: Car reaches the flag on the right hill or 200 steps elapse.

/api/envs.name: pendulum
/api/envs.label: Pendulum-v1
/api/envs.description: Balance an inverted pendulum by applying torque. Continuous torque in [-2,2] — prototypical continuous control.
/api/envs.termination_desc: 200 steps (no early termination).

/api/envs.name: mountain_car_continuous
/api/envs.label: MountainCarContinuous-v0
/api/envs.description: The continuous-torque version of Mountain Car. Instead of three discrete thrusts you apply a real-valued force in [-1, 1], and the magnitude of that force is penalised - so the agent must learn to be both effective and efficient.
/api/envs.reward_desc: +100 for reaching the goal, minus the sum of squared actions over the episode. Step reward is 0 otherwise.
/api/envs.termination_desc: Reaching the goal flag or 999 steps.

/api/envs.name: ant
/api/envs.label: Ant-v4
/api/envs.description: A 3D quadruped with 8 joints must learn to walk/run forward. Contact dynamics make it substantially richer than the 2D runners.
/api/envs.reward_desc: Forward velocity - control cost - contact cost + alive bonus while the torso stays healthy.
/api/envs.termination_desc: Unhealthy state (torso height/angle out of range, non-finite observation) or 1000 steps.

/api/envs.name: half_cheetah
/api/envs.label: HalfCheetah-v4
/api/envs.description: A 2-dimensional 'cheetah' with a fixed torso and two legs (6 joints) must learn to run forward as fast as possible. The standard sample-efficiency benchmark for continuous control.
/api/envs.reward_desc: Forward velocity reward minus a quadratic control cost.
/api/envs.termination_desc: Fixed 1000-step horizon (no 'unhealthy' termination, which is why it's more forgiving than Hopper/Walker2d).

/api/envs.name: hopper
/api/envs.label: Hopper-v4
/api/envs.description: A 2D one-legged robot (3 joints) must hop forward without falling. Adds a 'stay healthy' constraint that HalfCheetah lacks, so a bad policy terminates early instead of just scoring badly.
/api/envs.reward_desc: Forward velocity - control cost + a +1 alive bonus while the torso height and joint angles stay in the healthy range.
/api/envs.termination_desc: Unhealthy state (torso too low/high, joint out of range, or non-finite observation) or 1000 steps.

/api/envs.name: humanoid
/api/envs.label: Humanoid-v4
/api/envs.description: A 3D humanoid with 17 joints must learn to walk forward. The highest-dimensional control task in the suite (376-dim observations) and a genuine test of algorithm scalability.
/api/envs.reward_desc: Forward velocity - control cost - impact cost + alive bonus while the torso remains healthy.
/api/envs.termination_desc: Unhealthy state (torso height out of range, non-finite observation) or 1000 steps.

/api/envs.name: humanoid_standup
/api/envs.label: HumanoidStandup-v4

/api/envs.reward_desc: Shaped reward for raising the torso, minus control and impact costs.
/api/envs.termination_desc: Fixed 1000-step horizon (no unhealthy termination).

/api/envs.name: inverted_double_pendulum
/api/envs.label: InvertedDoublePendulum-v4
/api/envs.description: Two-link pendulum balanced on a sliding cart. A single continuous force must control a much less stable system than InvertedPendulum - the second link makes the dynamics genuinely harder.
/api/envs.reward_desc: Alive bonus plus quadratic penalties on the pole angles and their velocities; the agent is pushed toward a tight, still equilibrium.
/api/envs.termination_desc: Either link tilts too far, the cart leaves the rail, or 1000 steps elapse.

/api/envs.name: inverted_pendulum
/api/envs.label: InvertedPendulum-v4
/api/envs.description: MuJoCo's continuous-force version of CartPole. A cart slides along a rail and you apply a horizontal force to keep the pole upright. The gentlest possible introduction to continuous control.
/api/envs.reward_desc: +1 alive bonus for every step the pole stays within ~0.2 rad of vertical and the cart stays on the rail.
/api/envs.termination_desc: Pole angle leaves the healthy range, the cart slides off the rail, or 1000 steps elapse.

/api/envs.name: pusher
/api/envs.label: Pusher-v4
/api/envs.description: A 7-DOF arm pushes a cylinder across a table toward a target site. Harder than Reacher because the reward is a sum of three competing distances (hand-to-object, object-to-target, control cost).
/api/envs.reward_desc: -(distance fingertip to object) - (distance object to target) - control cost.

/api/envs.description: A two-link planar arm must touch a randomly placed target. Short, well-shaped episodes make it a friendly manipulation task.

/api/envs.termination_desc: Fixed 50-step horizon - there is no early termination.

docs.beginner: This agent flips coins. It never learns - and that is exactly why it is useful: it tells you what a 'no skill' score looks like on any environment, and it exercises every environment pathway without touching any learning code.
docs.technical: Samples uniformly from valid actions each step. No parameters, no state.
docs.intuition: Every trained agent should comfortably beat this line; if it doesn't, something is broken.
docs.pseudocode: for each step: action ~ Uniform(valid actions)
docs.exploration: Maximum possible - pure randomness forever.
failure_modes: None - but never mistake its score for a learned policy.

expected_metrics.meaning: Return accumulated this episode.

docs.math:
**Origin:** Baseline (Sutton & Barto, 2018). No learning — uniform $\pi(a|s)=1/|A|$.

**Formula:** $a_t \sim \mathcal{U}(A)$

**Where it comes from:** Sanity check; any learner must beat $\mathbb{E}[R]$ of random.

docs.beginner: Instead of a neural network this agent keeps a literal table of numbers: one row per state, one column per action. After every step it nudges the entry for what it just did toward the reward it observed plus the value of the next state. Q-learning always learns toward the best imagined next action, whether or not it actually takes it - it is 'off-policy'.
docs.technical: Update rule Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[r + γ·max_a′ Q(s′,a′) − Q(s,a)] (off-policy TD control, Watkins' variant with Q(λ)=0 behaviour). States are identified by the argmax of one-hot observations; unseen entries initialise to optimistic 0. Epsilon decays linearly per episode.
docs.intuition: The table is a cheat-sheet being graded after every single move. Values flow backwards from rewards one step at a time until early actions 'know' about distant goals.
docs.update_rule: Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α [ r + γ max_{a'} Q(s′,a') − Q(s,a) ]
docs.pseudocode:
for each episode:
    s = env.reset()
    while not done:
        a = eps-greedy(Q[s])
        s2, r, done = env.step(a)
        Q[s,a] += alpha*(r + gamma*max(Q[s2]) - Q[s,a])
        s = s2
docs.lifecycle:
1. Pick an action epsilon-greedily from the table row.
2. Step the environment.
3. Apply the one-step tabular update immediately.
4. Anneal epsilon at the end of each episode.
docs.learns: An explicit |states| × |actions| table of Q-values.
docs.exploration: Linear epsilon-greedy decay per episode.
docs.replay_buffer: Not used - tabular updates are applied online.
docs.networks: None - pure lookup table (no torch parameters).
failure_modes: State space must be small; continuous inputs get coarse-hashed
Max operator can propagate overly-optimistic values in noisy environments
Never explores states its policy avoids once epsilon is low

docs.beginner: Every real experience is written into a notebook: 'in state s, doing a gave reward r and led to s′'. Between real steps the agent flips through the notebook and practises on remembered experiences. In a deterministic world this is like getting many free episodes per real one.
docs.technical: Direct RL: one-step Q-learning on each real transition. Model learning: a table Model(s,a) = (r, s′, done) (last observed outcome). Planning: n times per step, sample a previously seen (s,a), query the model and apply the same Q-learning update (Sutton, 1990).

docs.beginner: DQN learns the *value* of taking each action in each situation (called a Q-value). docs.intuition: Q(s,a) answers: 'if I do a here, how much reward can I collect from now on?' If you know this table for every state, acting greedily on it is optimal. for each episode:

        buffer.add(s, a, r, s2, done)
        batch = buffer.sample(B)
        y = r + gamma * max Q_target(s2) * (1-done)

docs.beginner: Ordinary DQN replays its memories uniformly at random, so a rare, important moment (the first time the agent scores) is replayed as often as a boring one. Prioritised replay remembers how surprised the network was by each memory and revisits surprising ones more.
docs.technical: Sampling probability P(i) = p_i^α / Σ p^α with p_i = |δ_i| + ε. The bias this introduces is corrected with importance weights w_i = (N·P(i))^{-β} / max w, β annealed to 1 over training. New transitions get the current maximum priority so each is seen at least once (Schaul et al., 2016). Proportional variant, O(N) sampling.
docs.intuition: Study the questions you got wrong, not the ones you already know.
docs.update_rule: P(i) ∝ (|δ_i| + ε)^α ;  L = Σ_i w_i · huber(δ_i) ,  w_i = (N P(i))^{−β}

batch, idx, P = buffer.sample_proportional(B, alpha)
w = (N * P) ** -beta;  w /= w.max()
delta = y - Q(s, a)
minimise mean(w * huber(delta))
buffer.priorities[idx] = |delta| + eps

docs.beginner: REINFORCE is the simplest policy-gradient method: it directly nudges the probability of actions that led to good episode returns. After every full episode it looks at everything that happened and pushes probabilities up for good trajectories and down for bad ones.
docs.technical: Monte-Carlo returns G_t are computed by backward discounting; returns are then standardised per episode. The loss is −Σ log π(a_t|s_t)·Ĝ_t plus an entropy bonus (−entropy_coef · H[π]). Adam, grad-norm clip 10.
docs.intuition: Think of the policy as a habit strength for each action in each situation. REINFORCE reinforces habits that were followed by high reward - literally 'reinforcement' learning.
docs.update_rule: θ ← θ + α · Σ_t ∇θ log π_θ(a_t|s_t) · G_t
docs.pseudocode:
for each episode:
    trajectory = []
    roll out π until done
    G = 0
    for (s,a,r) in reversed(trajectory):
        G = r + gamma * G
        store (s, a, G)
    normalise returns
    loss = -Σ log π(a|s) * G - c*H[π]
    update θ with one gradient step

docs.math:
**Origin:** Williams 1992 REINFORCE.

**Baseline variant:** subtract $b(s)=V(s)$ → $G_t - b(s_t)$ reduces variance.

Loss = policy_loss + value_coef·value_loss − entropy_coef·H[π], where policy_loss = −Σ log π(a_t|s_t)·Â_t and value_loss = MSE(V(s_t), G_t). Shared-trunk MLP, Adam, grad-norm clip at max_grad_norm.
docs.intuition: The critic turns 'was the total reward good?' into 'was this move better than I expected?'. Learning from surprise rather than raw score is what makes actor-critic methods sample-efficient.

docs.beginner: PPO collects a batch of experience, then squeezes several careful improvement steps out of it. The famous 'clip' prevents any single update from changing the policy too much, which is what makes PPO famously stable and forgiving to tune.
docs.technical: Advantages via GAE(λ). The clipped surrogate L = E[min(r_t·Â_t, clip(r_t, 1±ε)·Â_t)] with probability ratio r_t = π_new/π_old. Value targets are GAE returns; total loss adds entropy bonus and value MSE. K epochs of shuffled minibatch Adam updates per rollout.
docs.intuition: Trust regions without second-order optimisation: improve confidently, but never move so far that your data stops describing your policy.
docs.update_rule: L^{CLIP} = Ê[min(r_t Â_t, clip(r_t, 1−ε, 1+ε) Â_t)]

repeat:

    compute GAE(λ) advantages & returns
    for epoch in 1..K:
        for minibatch:
            r = exp(logπ_new(a|s) - logπ_old(a|s))
            L_pol = -min(r*A, clamp(r,1±eps)*A)
            L_val = mse(V(s), G)
            step on L_pol + c_v*L_val - c_e*H[π]

docs.beginner: The same PPO as for button presses, but each action is a number on a dial. The policy proposes a most likely setting and a spread around it; training moves the setting toward what worked and narrows the spread as the agent becomes confident.
docs.technical: π(a|s) = N(μ_θ(s), diag(σ²)) with log σ a free parameter. The clipped surrogate, GAE(λ) and value loss are identical to discrete PPO; the log-probability is summed over action dimensions. Actions are sampled in [-1, 1] and affinely rescaled to the environment's bounds; the unclipped sample is stored so the log-probability stays exact.
docs.intuition: Start with a wide, uncertain dial; let evidence narrow it.

docs.math:
**Origin:** Schulman et al. 2017, with a Gaussian policy as in their MuJoCo experiments.

**Policy:** $\pi_\theta(a|s)=\mathcal{N}(\mu_\theta(s),\,\mathrm{diag}(\sigma^2))$ with $\log\sigma$ a free parameter, and $\log\pi(a|s)=\sum_i \log \mathcal{N}(a_i;\mu_i,\sigma_i)$.

**Objective:** $L^{CLIP}=\mathbb{E}_t[\min(r_t\hat A_t,\ \mathrm{clip}(r_t,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat A_t)]$ with $r_t=\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)/\pi_{old}(a_t|s_t)$ and $\hat A_t$ from GAE($\lambda$).

**Bounds:** sampling happens in $[-1,1]$; the environment receives $a_{env}=l+(\mathrm{clip}(a,-1,1)+1)(h-l)/2$, and the unclipped $a$ is kept for $\log\pi$.

docs.beginner: SAC keeps a slow-moving copy of its critic so its learning targets do not jump around, which also slows learning. CrossQ removes the copy and keeps things stable a different way: it normalises the critic's inputs and features over each batch.
docs.technical: Critic: Q(s,a) with BatchNorm after the input and each hidden layer. The TD target uses the same critic, evaluated in one forward pass on the concatenation of (s, a) and (s', a'~π), so batch statistics are shared: y = r + γ(1−d)(min Q(s',a') − α log π(a'|s')), with gradients stopped through the target half. No target network, no Polyak averaging. Adam β1 = 0.5, actor updated every 3 critic steps.
docs.intuition: Stability from normalisation instead of from deliberately lagging targets.
docs.update_rule: [Q(s,a), Q(s',a')] = Q_BN([s;s'], [a;a'])  ;  y = r + γ(1−d)(min Q(s',a') − α log π)
docs.pseudocode:
for each step:
    a' ~ π(s')
    q, q_next = critic(concat(s, s'), concat(a, a'))   # one batch-normalised pass
    y = r + γ(1-done)(min(q_next).detach() - α log π(a'|s'))
    critic loss = (q - y)^2
    every 3 steps: actor and temperature as in SAC
docs.learns: An actor, twin batch-normalised critics and the temperature α.
docs.exploration: Stochastic policy with automatic entropy tuning, as in SAC.
docs.networks: Gaussian actor (MLP); twin critics with BatchNorm layers.

Slower per update than SAC because the critics are wider

docs.beginner: First, learn how the world responds to actions: watch what happens and fit a model. Then, before every move, try hundreds of possible futures in your head, and do the first step of the best one. Next step, think again.
docs.technical: An ensemble of E networks predicts (Δs, r, done) from (s, a), each on a bootstrap of the data. Planning uses the cross-entropy method over H-step action sequences: sample a population, score each by its imagined discounted return (each particle follows one member: trajectory sampling), refit the sampling distribution to the elite, repeat. Execute the first action, replan next step (model-predictive control).
docs.intuition: Think before you act, using what you have learned about cause and effect.
docs.update_rule: a_t = first action of argmax_{a_{t:t+H}} Σ_k γ^k r̂_k under the learned model
docs.pseudocode:
repeat each episode:
    for each step:
        dist = N(mean, std) over H-step action sequences
        repeat K times:
            plans = sample(dist);  score = imagined return of each plan
            dist = fit(top plans by score)
        act(first action of best plan)
    train the ensemble on all real transitions

docs.math:
**Origin:** Chua, Calandra, McAllister & Levine, NeurIPS 2018.

**Model:** an ensemble $\{f_{\theta_e}\}_{e=1}^{E}$ trained on bootstrapped data to predict $\Delta s = s_{t+1} - s_t$, the reward and termination from $(s_t, a_t)$. Disagreement between members approximates epistemic uncertainty.

**Planning (MPC):** at every step solve $\max_{a_{t:t+H}} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{H-1} \gamma^k \hat r_{t+k}\right]$ approximately with the cross-entropy method, execute $a_t$ only, and replan.

**CEM:** sample $N$ sequences from $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$, keep the top $K$ by imagined return, set $\mu, \sigma$ to their mean and spread, repeat.

docs.technical: From real start states, roll the learned model forward H steps under the actor. The critic regresses λ-returns of imagined rewards; the actor maximises them, by backpropagating through the differentiable model for continuous actions (dynamics backpropagation) or by REINFORCE with the critic as baseline for discrete ones. Dreamer adds a learned latent space for pixels; this version works on state vectors.

    train the model on real data
    repeat N times:
        s = real states;  imagine H steps with actor and model
        critic -> λ-returns;  actor -> maximise λ-returns

docs.math:
**Origin:** Hafner et al., *Dream to Control* (2020), *DreamerV3* (2023); here without the latent image model.

**λ-returns in imagination:** $G_t^\lambda = \hat r_t + \gamma \hat c_t\left[(1-\lambda) V(\hat s_{t+1}) + \lambda G_{t+1}^\lambda\right]$, with $\hat c_t$ the predicted probability of continuing.

**Actor:** continuous actions maximise $\mathbb{E}[G^\lambda]$ by backpropagating through the differentiable model (dynamics backpropagation); discrete actions use $\nabla \log \pi(a\mid s)\,(G^\lambda - V(s))$.

**Critic:** $\min_\psi \mathbb{E}\left[(V_\psi(\hat s_t) - G_t^\lambda)^2\right]$ on imagined states.

docs.beginner: DDPG keeps two networks. The 'critic' estimates how good a particular action is in a particular situation; the 'actor' directly outputs the action to take. The actor is trained by asking the critic 'which way should I change my output to get a higher score?' and following that gradient. Because the policy is deterministic, exploration has to be bolted on: DDPG adds random noise to the action it executes.
docs.technical: Critic minimises MSE(Q(s,a), r + gamma * Q_target(s2, mu_target(s2)) * (1-done)). Actor maximises Q(s, mu(s)). Both target networks are updated by Polyak averaging with coefficient tau every gradient step. Actions are stored in the buffer normalised to [-1,1] and rescaled to the environment's bounds when executed. Observations are optionally whitened with running mean/std.
docs.intuition: Instead of scoring every possible action and picking the best, learn a direct 'state -> action' mapping, and use the critic's gradient as the training signal for that mapping.
docs.update_rule: y = r + γ · Q̄(s′, μ̄(s′)) · (1 − done);   L_critic = (Q(s,a) − y)²;   L_actor = −Q(s, μ(s))
docs.pseudocode:
for each environment step:
    a = mu(s) + noise                  # clipped to the action range
    s2, r, done = env.step(a)
    buffer.add(s, a, r, s2, done)
    batch = buffer.sample(B)
    y = r + gamma * Q_target(s2, mu_target(s2)) * (1-done)
    update critic to minimise (Q(s,a) - y)^2
    update actor to maximise Q(s, mu(s))
    soft-update both target networks: target <- (1-tau)*target + tau*online

2. Store the normalised transition in the replay buffer.
3. After `warmup_steps`, take `updates_per_step` gradient steps per environment step.
4. Soft-update the target actor and critic every gradient step.
5. Optionally anneal the exploration noise across training.

docs.beginner: TD3 is DDPG with three fixes for problems researchers kept hitting. (1) It trains two critics and always believes the more pessimistic one, which stops the agent fooling itself about how good an action is. (2) It updates the actor less often than the critic, so the policy does not chase a value estimate that is still moving. (3) When scoring the next state it adds a little noise to the action, which stops the agent exploiting narrow spikes in its own value estimate.
docs.technical: y = r + gamma * (1-done) * min_{i=1,2} Q_target_i(s2, a2), where a2 = clip(mu_target(s2) + clip(N(0, sigma), -c, c), -1, 1). The critic is updated every step; the actor and all target networks are updated only every `policy_delay` steps (the paper's delayed policy updates).
docs.intuition: Be pessimistic about value, be patient about changing the policy, and smooth the target so a narrow spike in the critic cannot be exploited.
docs.update_rule:
a2 = clip(μ̄(s′) + clip(ε, −c, c), −1, 1),  ε ~ N(0, σ);
y = r + γ · (1 − done) · min_{i=1,2} Q̄_i(s′, a2)
docs.pseudocode:
for each environment step:
    a = mu(s) + N(0, expl_noise)
    s2, r, done = env.step(a)
    buffer.add(s, a, r, s2, done)
    batch = buffer.sample(B)
    a2 = clip(mu_target(s2) + clip(N(0, target_noise), -c, c), -1, 1)
    y = r + gamma * (1-done) * min(Q1_target(s2,a2), Q2_target(s2,a2))
    update both critics towards y
    if step % policy_delay == 0:
        update actor to maximise Q1(s, mu(s))
        soft-update all three target networks
docs.lifecycle:
1. Act with the deterministic policy plus Gaussian noise.
2. Store the normalised transition.
3. Update both critics every gradient step against the clipped double-Q target.
4. Every `policy_delay` steps, update the actor and soft-sync the targets.
5. Repeat; noise is not annealed by default.

docs.advantage: Not used - twin critics replace the need for a baseline.
docs.networks: Actor: obs -> 256 -> ReLU -> 256 -> ReLU -> tanh -> action. Two critics: (obs, action) -> 256 -> ReLU -> 256 -> ReLU -> 1.
failure_modes: Still deterministic at evaluation time - on genuinely stochastic tasks a stochastic policy (SAC) can be better
Too large `expl_noise` prevents the policy from ever consolidating
Delayed updates mean slower adaptation if `policy_delay` is set high

docs.beginner: SAC changes the objective: instead of only maximising reward, it maximises reward *plus randomness*. Staying as unpredictable as possible while still doing well forces the agent to keep trying alternatives instead of committing too early, which turns out to be a very effective form of exploration. Best of all, the amount of randomness to aim for is learned automatically, so there is one fewer knob to tune.
docs.technical: Policy is a squashed Gaussian sampled with the reparameterisation trick. Critic targets use the clipped double-Q minimum minus the entropy bonus: y = r + gamma*(1-done)*(min_i Q_target_i(s2,a2) - alpha*log pi(a2|s2)) with a2 ~ pi(.|s2). The actor minimises alpha*log pi(a|s) - min_i Q_i(s,a). With `auto_entropy` the temperature alpha is learned by minimising -alpha*(log pi + H_target), H_target = -target_entropy_scale * act_dim.
docs.intuition: Reward the policy for being uncertain. A policy that is forced to stay somewhat random keeps exploring, and 'good but random' is a much easier target to hit than a single perfect deterministic answer.
docs.update_rule:
y = r + γ(1−done)·( min_i Q̄_i(s′,a′) − α·log π(a′|s′) ),  a′ ~ π(·|s′)
L_actor = α·log π(a|s) − min_i Q_i(s,a);   L_α = −α·(log π(a|s) + H_target)
docs.pseudocode:
for each environment step:
    a ~ pi(.|s)                        # tanh-Gaussian sample
    s2, r, done = env.step(a)
    buffer.add(s, a, r, s2, done)
    batch = buffer.sample(B)
    a2, logp2 = pi(.|s2)               # with reparameterisation
    y = r + gamma*(1-done)*(min(Q1t,Q2t)(s2,a2) - alpha*logp2)
    update both critics towards y
    a_new, logp = pi(.|s)
    update actor to maximise min(Q1,Q2)(s,a_new) - alpha*logp
    if auto_entropy: update alpha towards target entropy
    soft-update both target critics (SAC has no target actor)
docs.lifecycle:
1. Sample an action from the stochastic policy (or use tanh(mu) when evaluating).
2. Store the normalised transition.
3. After `warmup_steps`, take `updates_per_step` gradient steps per environment step: critics, then actor, then temperature.
4. Soft-update the two target critics every step.
5. There is no target actor - the bootstrap uses a freshly sampled action from the current policy.
docs.learns: A Gaussian actor (mean and log-std per action dim) plus two critics.
docs.exploration: Intrinsic: the policy is stochastic and is explicitly rewarded for entropy. No hand-tuned noise schedule is needed.
docs.replay_buffer: Uniform sampling from the last `buffer_size` transitions.
docs.target_network: Polyak soft update of the two target critics; unlike DDPG/TD3 there is no target actor.
docs.advantage: Not used - the entropy term acts as a learned, state-dependent bonus.
docs.networks: Actor: shared trunk obs -> 256 -> ReLU -> 256 -> ReLU, then separate mu and log-std heads, squashed with tanh. Two critics: (obs, action) -> 256 -> ReLU -> 256 -> ReLU -> 1.
failure_modes: With auto_entropy off, `alpha` becomes the critical hyperparameter and a bad value silently ruins learning
The log-std head can saturate at its clamp bounds on some tasks
Stochastic evaluation is noisier than a deterministic policy - the testbed evaluates with the mean action (tanh(mu)) for this reason

benchmarks.title: Policy sanity
benchmarks.tests: Can the implementation learn *anything*? One state, one action, constant +1 reward.
benchmarks.why: Catches broken optimisers, wrong loss signs, and pipeline bugs before you waste GPU-hours.
benchmarks.expected: Reward reaches 1.0 within a few dozen episodes for any working learner.
benchmarks.failure_suggests: A plumbing bug: gradients not applied, agent never updated, or env/agent mismatch.
benchmarks.how_to: Train any algorithm on probe1 for 30-50 episodes; every eval should equal 1.0.

benchmarks.title: State conditioning
benchmarks.tests: Does the policy depend on observations at all (action 1 always beats action 0)?
benchmarks.why: Detects blind policies - e.g. networks that ignore inputs or agents acting from stale buffers.
benchmarks.expected: Greedy eval converges to 1.0 as the agent reliably picks action 1.
benchmarks.failure_suggests: Observations are not reaching the network, or exploration noise dominates forever.
benchmarks.how_to: Train DQN on probe2, 50 episodes, then confirm greedy eval hits 1.0.

benchmarks.title: Delayed reward & credit assignment
benchmarks.tests: Two-step chain where only the second action pays out (+1). Requires correct discount propagation.
benchmarks.why: The essence of RL is propagating future reward to earlier decisions. This verifies bootstrapping/discounting.
benchmarks.expected: Agent learns action sequence [0 then 1]; eval reward → 1.0.
benchmarks.failure_suggests: gamma too low, targets computed without next-state values, or returns misaligned by an offset.
benchmarks.how_to: Train DQN (γ=0.9+) or Q-learning on probe3 for 100-200 episodes.

benchmarks.title: Stochastic rewards
benchmarks.tests: Same state/action pair yields different rewards (p=0.8 vs p=0.2 arms).
benchmarks.why: Real environments are noisy. This checks value estimates converge through variance instead of oscillating.
benchmarks.expected: Slower but steady convergence toward preferring action 1; loss stays bounded.
benchmarks.failure_suggests: Learning rate too high for the noise level, or no averaging in updates.
benchmarks.how_to: Train DQN 200 episodes on probe4; mean reward should exceed 0.6.

benchmarks.title: Exploration vs exploitation
benchmarks.tests: Classic two-armed bandit (arms pay 0.8 / 0.2). Pure exploitation of early luck fails.
benchmarks.why: Verifies the exploration mechanism samples enough to find the better arm.
benchmarks.expected: With healthy epsilon decay the agent locks onto arm 1; eval ≈ 0.8.
benchmarks.failure_suggests: Epsilon decayed too fast, or entropy bonus too weak.
benchmarks.how_to: Train DQN 300 episodes on probe5 with default epsilon schedule.

benchmarks.title: Continuous control sanity
benchmarks.tests: One step, one continuous action in [-1, 1]; reward 1 - |a - 0.5|.
benchmarks.why: The only probe continuous-action learners can run. Checks action scaling, bound handling and that the policy moves toward higher reward.
benchmarks.expected: The greedy action settles within 0.1 of 0.5, so evaluation reward exceeds 0.9.
benchmarks.failure_suggests: Actions not rescaled to the bounds, a squashing bug, or exploration noise left on during evaluation.
benchmarks.how_to: Train SAC on probe6 for 300 episodes; evaluation should exceed 0.9.

/api/glossary.definition: The learner: it observes, chooses actions, and improves from the rewards it gets.
/api/glossary.detail: In the testbed an agent is one algorithm with its own parameters and memory. It sees only observations and rewards, never the environment's internals.

/api/glossary.definition: The world the agent acts in: it returns the next observation and a reward for every action.
/api/glossary.detail: Each environment defines what can be observed, which actions exist, how rewards are paid, and when an episode ends. The testbed groups environments into labs by the shape of the problem they pose.

/api/glossary.definition: The mathematical model behind most RL: states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards and a discount.
/api/glossary.detail: "Markov" means the next state depends only on the current state and action, not on the history. When the agent cannot see the full state (as in poker), the problem is partially observable and memory starts to matter.

/api/glossary.definition: The state is the full situation of the environment; the observation is what the agent gets to see of it.
/api/glossary.detail: In Gridworld they coincide: the agent knows its cell. In MuJoCo the observation is a vector of joint angles and velocities. In Texas Hold'em the opponent's cards are part of the state but not of the observation. The Visualize page shows exactly what the agent observes.

/api/glossary.definition: A vector of zeros with a single 1 marking which of N discrete states (or categories) applies.
/api/glossary.detail: Tabular environments hand the agent its state this way. It carries no notion of distance: state 3 is no more similar to state 4 than to state 40, so nothing learned in one state transfers to its neighbours.

/api/glossary.definition: What the agent does at each step: a choice from a list (discrete) or a vector of numbers (continuous).
/api/glossary.detail: CartPole has two discrete actions, push left or push right. HalfCheetah's action is six joint torques between -1 and 1. Algorithms are built for one kind or the other, which is why the testbed checks compatibility before a run starts.

/api/glossary.definition: A list of which actions are legal right now; mask-aware algorithms never choose an illegal one.
/api/glossary.detail: In Connect Four a full column cannot take another disc. The environment sends a mask with every observation, and the agent sets the probability (or value) of illegal actions to nothing before choosing.

/api/glossary.definition: A number the environment returns after each action; the agent's only signal of what is good.
/api/glossary.detail: Rewards define the task. CartPole pays +1 for every step the pole stays up; CliffWalking charges -1 per step and -100 for falling. Changing the reward changes what is optimal.

/api/glossary.definition: One run of the environment from reset to an end: termination (the task ended) or truncation (a time limit).
/api/glossary.detail: Learning curves plot one point per episode. The distinction matters for learning: at termination the future is worth nothing, while at truncation the agent was simply cut off.

/api/glossary.definition: Termination: the task really ended (the pole fell). Truncation: a time limit cut the episode short.
/api/glossary.detail: The difference matters for learning. After termination the future is worth nothing, so the target is just the reward. After truncation the world would have continued, so the target must still include the value of the next state. Treating Pendulum's 200-step limit as termination teaches an agent that its final state is worthless.

/api/glossary.definition: The sequence of states, actions and rewards produced by acting in an environment.
/api/glossary.detail: Visualize plays one trajectory step by step. Monte Carlo methods learn from whole trajectories; temporal-difference methods learn from single steps of them.

/api/glossary.definition: The total (discounted) reward from a time step to the end of the episode: what the agent tries to maximise.
/api/glossary.detail: Learning curves plot the return of each training episode. Because exploration adds noise, the testbed also plots a greedy evaluation every few episodes.

/api/glossary.definition: γ in [0, 1): how much a reward one step later is worth compared with one now.
/api/glossary.detail: It sets the agent's effective planning horizon, roughly $1/(1-\gamma)$ steps: 0.99 looks about 100 steps ahead, 0.9 about 10. Too low and long-term goals become invisible; too high and learning slows and becomes noisier.

/api/glossary.definition: The agent's behaviour: a rule that maps each observation to an action, or to probabilities over actions.
/api/glossary.detail: A deterministic policy picks one action per state; a stochastic policy samples from a distribution. Policy-gradient methods learn the policy directly; value-based methods derive it from learned values by acting greedily.

/api/glossary.definition: V(s): the return the agent can expect from state s if it follows its policy from there.
/api/glossary.detail: Values turn a sparse, delayed reward into a signal available in every state. A critic in actor-critic methods is a learned value function.

/api/glossary.definition: Q(s, a): the expected return from taking action a in state s and following the policy afterwards.
/api/glossary.detail: Knowing Q makes acting easy: pick the action with the highest value. Q-learning, SARSA and DQN all learn Q; tabular methods store it in a table, DQN approximates it with a network.

/api/glossary.definition: The recursive relation that values satisfy: a state's value is the immediate reward plus the discounted value of what follows.
/api/glossary.detail: Nearly every value-based method is a way of making its estimates satisfy this equation. The optimality version, with a max over next actions, is what Q-learning chases.

/api/glossary.definition: The action with the highest estimated value right now.
/api/glossary.detail: Always acting greedily never tests whether another action is better, so learners mix in exploration during training. Evaluations in the testbed use greedy actions to measure what has been learned without that noise.

/api/glossary.definition: The trade-off between trying actions to learn about them and choosing the action that currently looks best.
/api/glossary.detail: Too little exploration and the agent settles on the first decent behaviour it finds; too much and it never benefits from what it knows. Bandits isolate this trade-off.

/api/glossary.definition: With probability ε take a random action, otherwise the greedy one. ε usually decays during training.
/api/glossary.detail: Simple and effective, but blind: it explores a hopeless action as often as a promising one. Watch the epsilon metric on a run to see the schedule.

/api/glossary.definition: Explore by optimism: add a bonus to each action's value that shrinks the more often it has been tried.
/api/glossary.detail: Rarely tried actions look attractive until there is evidence about them, so exploration is directed rather than random, and there is no ε to tune.

/api/glossary.definition: Keep a probability distribution over each action's value, sample one value per action, and act greedily on the samples.
/api/glossary.detail: Each action is chosen with roughly the probability that it is the best one. Uncertain actions sometimes draw high samples and get tried; as evidence grows they stop.

/api/glossary.definition: The reward lost by not always choosing the best action: the standard measure of exploration quality.
/api/glossary.detail: A good exploration strategy has regret that grows ever more slowly. Comparing cumulative return of UCB and ε-greedy on a bandit is a direct look at regret.

/api/glossary.definition: The environment changes over time, so old experience becomes misleading.
/api/glossary.detail: Sample averages weigh all of history equally and fall behind; a constant step size weighs recent experience more. The Drifting Bandit makes the difference visible.

/api/glossary.definition: α: how far each update moves an estimate toward its target.
/api/glossary.detail: Large steps learn fast but noisily and can diverge; small steps are stable but slow. In deep RL the learning rate of the optimiser plays this role and is often the most sensitive hyperparameter, which is what sweeps are for.

/api/glossary.definition: Learn from complete episodes: move each estimate toward the return that actually followed.
/api/glossary.detail: Unbiased, since it uses real returns, but high variance, and nothing is learned until an episode ends.

/api/glossary.definition: Learn from single steps: move an estimate toward the reward plus the estimated value of the next state.
/api/glossary.detail: TD methods learn during the episode and usually faster than Monte Carlo, at the price of some bias from trusting their own estimates.

/api/glossary.definition: δ: the gap between an estimate and its one-step target. Most value methods try to shrink it.
/api/glossary.detail: A TD error that never falls points to a bug or too high a learning rate. Tabular agents report it as the td_error metric.

/api/glossary.definition: Updating an estimate from another estimate, instead of waiting for the true return.
/api/glossary.detail: It is what lets TD methods learn mid-episode, and also what lets errors feed on themselves: a wrong value of the next state becomes a wrong target for this one.

/api/glossary.definition: Learn about the policy you are currently following, so data must come from that policy.
/api/glossary.detail: SARSA, REINFORCE, A2C and PPO are on-policy. They cannot reuse old experience after the policy changes, which makes them less sample-efficient but often more stable.

/api/glossary.definition: Learn about one policy (usually the greedy one) from data collected by another (usually an exploring one).
/api/glossary.detail: Q-learning, DQN, SAC and TD3 are off-policy, which is what allows replay buffers. On CliffWalking, off-policy Q-learning learns the risky edge path that is optimal only once exploration stops; on-policy SARSA learns the safer path it can actually follow.

/api/glossary.definition: Working out which earlier actions deserve credit for a reward that arrives later.
/api/glossary.detail: The longer the delay, the harder it is. Discounting, bootstrapping and eligibility techniques like GAE are all ways of spreading credit back in time.

/api/glossary.definition: Almost every step pays nothing, so the agent gets little signal until it stumbles on success.
/api/glossary.detail: MountainCar pays only at the flag. Random exploration rarely gets there, so curves stay flat for a long time and then jump.

/api/glossary.definition: Representing values or policies with a parameterised function, such as a neural network, instead of a table.
/api/glossary.detail: Tables cannot handle continuous or huge state spaces and learn nothing about unseen states. A network generalises between similar states, at the cost of stability: targets and estimates now share parameters.

/api/glossary.definition: A memory of past transitions that an off-policy learner samples from for each update.
/api/glossary.detail: Sampling at random breaks the correlation between consecutive steps and reuses each experience many times. The buffer_size metric shows it filling.

/api/glossary.definition: Replay transitions in proportion to how surprising they were (their TD error).
/api/glossary.detail: Rare, informative transitions get revisited more often. Importance-sampling weights correct the bias this introduces.

/api/glossary.definition: A slowly updated copy of the network used to compute training targets.
/api/glossary.detail: Without it the target moves with every gradient step, and the network chases its own tail. DQN copies the weights every few hundred updates; SAC and TD3 blend them in slowly.

/api/glossary.definition: Taking the maximum of noisy estimates systematically picks lucky ones, so learned values drift upward.
/api/glossary.detail: Double Q-learning and Double DQN separate choosing the best action from evaluating it; TD3 and SAC take the minimum of two critics.

/api/glossary.definition: A Q-network split into a state-value stream and an advantage stream, recombined into Q.
/api/glossary.detail: Many states have values that barely depend on the action; learning V separately makes those states cheaper to learn.

/api/glossary.definition: Learn the whole distribution of returns rather than only its mean.
/api/glossary.detail: Two actions with the same average can carry very different risks. C51 represents the distribution with 51 bins; acting still uses the mean.

/api/glossary.definition: Improve the policy directly by following the gradient of expected return with respect to its parameters.
/api/glossary.detail: Actions that led to high return become more likely. Works naturally with stochastic and continuous policies, but raw estimates are noisy.

/api/glossary.definition: The simplest policy gradient: scale the log-probability gradient of each action by the return that followed.
/api/glossary.detail: Unbiased but high variance, which is why its learning curves look noisy and why baselines were invented.

/api/glossary.definition: A value subtracted from returns in the policy gradient to reduce variance without adding bias.
/api/glossary.detail: The usual choice is the state value V(s); what remains is the advantage. Compare REINFORCE with and without a baseline on CartPole over several seeds to see the variance drop.

/api/glossary.definition: How much better an action is than the policy's average in that state.
/api/glossary.detail: Positive advantage makes an action more likely, negative less. Using advantages instead of raw returns is the main variance reduction in actor-critic methods.

/api/glossary.definition: A policy (the actor) trained with the help of a learned value function (the critic) that judges its actions.
/api/glossary.detail: The critic supplies low-variance advantage estimates by bootstrapping; the actor uses them in a policy-gradient update. A2C, PPO, SAC and TD3 are all actor-critic methods.

/api/glossary.definition: An advantage estimate that blends n-step estimates with weights decaying by γλ.
/api/glossary.detail: λ trades bias for variance: 0 gives the one-step TD advantage (low variance, biased), 1 gives Monte Carlo returns minus a baseline (unbiased, noisy). 0.95 is the usual compromise.

/api/glossary.definition: A term rewarding the policy for staying random, which keeps it exploring.
/api/glossary.detail: Policy entropy usually falls as training converges. Too large a bonus and the policy never commits; zero and it can collapse onto a poor action early.

/api/glossary.definition: Limit how far one update can change the policy by clipping the probability ratio.
/api/glossary.detail: Large policy steps can wreck a policy that took hours to learn. PPO stops the objective from rewarding changes beyond 1 ± ε, approximating TRPO's trust region with a simple loss.

/api/glossary.definition: A measure of how different two probability distributions are; used to track how far a policy moved.
/api/glossary.detail: PPO reports approx_kl per update. Values far above about 0.02 suggest updates are too aggressive (learning rate or epochs too high).

/api/glossary.definition: A stochastic policy for continuous actions: a network outputs a mean, and actions are sampled around it.
/api/glossary.detail: The spread (standard deviation) controls exploration and is usually learned. Gaussian PPO and SAC use one; SAC squashes samples through tanh to respect action bounds.

/api/glossary.definition: Improve a deterministic continuous policy by following the critic's gradient with respect to the action.
/api/glossary.detail: The actor learns to output actions the critic rates higher. DDPG and TD3 use it, adding noise to actions only for exploration.

/api/glossary.definition: Maximise reward plus the policy's entropy, weighted by a temperature α.
/api/glossary.detail: The agent is rewarded for achieving the task in as many ways as possible, which makes exploration robust. SAC tunes α automatically; its alpha metric shows the current value.

/api/glossary.definition: Passing sampled actions through tanh so they always lie within the environment's bounds.
/api/glossary.detail: Squashing changes the action's probability, so its log-probability needs a correction term; forgetting it is a classic SAC bug.

/api/glossary.definition: Rescaling each observation dimension by a running mean and standard deviation.
/api/glossary.detail: MuJoCo observations mix positions near 1 with velocities near 10; without normalisation the network sees mostly the large numbers. Off-policy agents must store raw observations and normalise when sampling: normalising at storage time leaves early samples scaled by statistics from a handful of steps. That bug kept the testbed's SAC from learning Pendulum until v3.7.

/api/glossary.definition: Replace target networks with batch-normalised critics that see current and next state-action pairs in one batch.
/api/glossary.detail: Target networks stabilise learning by lagging behind, which also slows it. CrossQ removes them: because current and next pairs are normalised together, the critic's targets stay consistent with its estimates. It matched or beat SAC's sample efficiency with less machinery.

/api/glossary.definition: An architecture of normalised residual blocks that keeps improving as it gets bigger, unlike plain MLPs in RL.
/api/glossary.detail: Bigger plain networks often learn worse in RL. SimBa's residual blocks with layer normalisation (plus observation normalisation) bias the network toward simple functions, so adding parameters helps. In the testbed it is the network option of SAC and TD3.

/api/glossary.definition: A learned or given predictor of the next state and reward for a state and action.
/api/glossary.detail: With a model the agent can imagine experience instead of collecting it. Model errors are the risk: the agent may exploit mistakes in its own model.

/api/glossary.definition: Improving a policy or values using a model, without acting in the real environment.
/api/glossary.detail: In Dyna-Q, planning means replaying remembered transitions and applying ordinary Q-learning updates to them.

/api/glossary.definition: An architecture that interleaves learning from real experience, learning a model, and planning with it.
/api/glossary.detail: Each real step is followed by n imagined updates. On the Dyna maze, 50 planning steps solve the task in a handful of real episodes.

/api/glossary.definition: A learned model of the environment that predicts what happens next, and what reward follows, for any action.
/api/glossary.detail: With a world model an agent can try actions in its head instead of in the world, which makes learning far more sample-efficient when real experience is slow or expensive. Its predictions are only as good as the data it was trained on.

/api/glossary.definition: Plan a sequence of actions in the model, execute only the first, then plan again from the new state.
/api/glossary.detail: Replanning every step corrects for model errors and surprises, at the cost of planning constantly. PETS and TD-MPC2 act this way; Dreamer instead trains a policy and only uses the model during training.

/api/glossary.definition: Optimise by sampling: draw many candidates, keep the best few, refit the sampling distribution to them, repeat.
/api/glossary.detail: PETS uses it to search over action sequences: no gradients needed, so any model and any reward will do. Each round concentrates the samples where imagined returns are highest.

/api/glossary.definition: Uncertainty from not having seen enough data, as opposed to randomness in the world itself.
/api/glossary.detail: An ensemble of models trained on different bootstrap samples agrees where data is plentiful and disagrees where it is not. PETS lets each imagined trajectory follow one member, so plans that rely on poorly understood regions score inconsistently.

/api/glossary.definition: Small one-step prediction errors grow as the model feeds its own predictions back in over many steps.
/api/glossary.detail: The Imagination tab on a world-model run shows it directly: the model tracks reality for a few steps, then drifts. It is why imagination horizons are short and why MPC replans.

/api/glossary.definition: Training a policy on trajectories generated by the world model instead of the real environment.
/api/glossary.detail: Dreamer starts imagined rollouts from real states and improves its actor and critic on them; real experience only keeps the model honest. Errors in the model become errors in the policy, so imagined returns can be optimistic.

/api/glossary.definition: Training a language model to predict text (pretraining) and then to imitate good answers (SFT), before any RL.
/api/glossary.detail: RL for language models never starts from scratch: it refines a model that already produces well-formed, partly correct answers. In the Language lab each task's base model is pretrained on demonstrations that are wrong half the time, so it knows the format but samples a correct answer only about half the time.

/api/glossary.definition: Fine-tuning a language model with rewards computed by a program that checks the answer, not by a learned judge.
/api/glossary.detail: Maths answers can be checked exactly, code can be run against tests. A verifier is hard to fool, which makes RLVR far more resistant to reward hacking than a learned reward model. It is how reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1 were trained.

/api/glossary.definition: Score each answer against the other answers sampled for the same prompt, instead of against a learned value.
/api/glossary.detail: GRPO samples G answers per prompt and uses each one's reward minus the group mean (divided by the group's spread) as its advantage, shared by all of its tokens. It needs no critic network. Groups where every answer scores the same carry no signal.

/api/glossary.term: KL penalty to a reference model
/api/glossary.definition: A penalty for drifting away from a frozen copy of the starting model, added to the RL objective.
/api/glossary.detail: It keeps the fine-tuned model close to what pretraining taught it, which preserves fluency and limits reward hacking. Too small and the policy exploits flaws in the reward; too large and it cannot improve. The testbed estimates it per token with the k3 estimator.

/api/glossary.definition: A learned or hand-written scorer that stands in for what people actually want.
/api/glossary.detail: In RLHF a network trained on human preferences scores answers. Every reward model is an imperfect proxy, and optimising a proxy hard enough finds where it is wrong.

/api/glossary.definition: The policy raises its reward by exploiting a flaw in the reward instead of doing the task better.
/api/glossary.detail: On the hackable addition task the reward also pays for length, so rambling earns more than being right: without a strong enough KL penalty, reward climbs to its maximum while true accuracy falls to zero. Exploits only appear once the policy can stumble on them.

/api/glossary.definition: Learn from pairs of answers where one is preferred, with no reward model and no RL sampling loop.
/api/glossary.detail: DPO solves the KL-regularised RL objective in closed form, turning it into a classification loss on preference pairs measured against the reference model.

/api/glossary.definition: GRPO with four refinements: clip-higher, dynamic sampling, a token-level loss, and no KL penalty.
/api/glossary.detail: Clip-higher lets the probability of unlikely-but-good tokens grow faster than PPO-style clipping allows, to counter entropy collapse. Dynamic sampling replaces groups whose answers all scored the same, since they carry no gradient. Both matter most in long training on hard problems; at the Language lab's scale the effects are small.

/api/glossary.definition: RL concentrating probability on answers the model could already produce, so one sample is right more often.
/api/glossary.detail: In the Language lab the base model's greedy answer is nearly always right but a single sample is right about half the time; RL with verifiable rewards closes that gap. Watch entropy fall as it happens. Whether RL also teaches genuinely new abilities is an open question.

/api/glossary.definition: The number that fixes every random draw in a run, making it reproducible.
/api/glossary.detail: Two seeds of the same configuration can produce very different curves. Results should be reported across several seeds; the testbed pools them into a mean with a ±1σ band.

/api/glossary.definition: How much results change between runs that differ only in their random seed.
/api/glossary.detail: RL is notoriously high-variance: a single lucky run can make a poor method look good. If two methods' bands overlap heavily, you cannot yet say one is better.

/api/glossary.definition: The shaded region around a mean curve, one standard deviation either side, across seeds.
/api/glossary.detail: It shows the spread of individual runs, not the uncertainty of the mean. The mean's own uncertainty, the standard error, shrinks with more seeds; the band does not.

/api/glossary.definition: A plot of performance (usually return) against training progress (episodes or steps).
/api/glossary.detail: Read its shape, not just its end: how quickly it rises, how noisy it is, whether it collapses. Smoothing helps the eye but hides individual episodes.

/api/glossary.definition: Measuring a policy with exploration switched off, separate from training episodes.
/api/glossary.detail: Training returns include the cost of exploring; evaluations show what has been learned. The testbed runs one every eval_freq episodes and plots them as a dashed line.

/api/glossary.definition: How much experience (environment steps) a method needs to reach a given performance.
/api/glossary.detail: Off-policy and model-based methods tend to be more sample-efficient; on-policy methods often need more steps but less tuning. Compare curves on the same x-axis.

/api/glossary.definition: The return at which a task counts as solved, as defined by the environment's authors.
/api/glossary.detail: CartPole is solved at a mean return of 475. Charts draw it as a dashed line; comparisons report how many episodes each configuration needed to reach it.

/api/glossary.definition: A setting chosen before training, such as the learning rate, discount or network size.
/api/glossary.detail: RL methods are often more sensitive to hyperparameters than to the choice of method. Change one at a time, and compare across seeds.

/api/glossary.definition: Running many configurations systematically to find good settings and learn how sensitive a method is.
/api/glossary.detail: Grid search tries every combination; random search samples them and usually finds good settings with fewer runs. The sweep page ranks configurations and shows each parameter's effect.

/api/glossary.definition: A tiny environment with a known answer that any correct implementation solves in seconds.
/api/glossary.detail: If an algorithm fails a probe, the problem is a bug or a setting, not task difficulty. Run them before trusting a new implementation.

/api/glossary.definition: A saved copy of an agent's parameters during or after training.
/api/glossary.detail: Runs save the best-evaluating checkpoint; Keep model copies it to Models so it can be re-evaluated or watched in Visualize after the run is deleted.

/api/learning-path.title: Meet the random agent
/api/learning-path.why: See what a 'no skill' baseline looks like and confirm your setup works end-to-end.
/api/learning-path.done_when: You can read a reward chart of a random run.

/api/learning-path.title: Run the diagnostic probes
/api/learning-path.why: Probes verify the learning machinery in seconds. If these fail, nothing else will work.
/api/learning-path.done_when: At least three probes converge as described in Benchmarks.

/api/learning-path.title: Tabular Q-learning on Gridworld
/api/learning-path.why: Watch a value table learn optimal paths - RL without neural-network opacity.
/api/learning-path.done_when: Episode lengths drop from ~50 to ~10 steps.

/api/learning-path.title: DQN on CartPole
/api/learning-path.why: The classic deep-RL starter: replay buffer + target network on a dense-reward task.

/api/learning-path.title: Policy gradients on CartPole
/api/learning-path.why: Compare how a policy-gradient method learns differently from DQN on the same task.
/api/learning-path.done_when: You can explain why its curve is noisier than DQN's.

/api/learning-path.title: PPO
/api/learning-path.why: PPO is the industry default. Learn its rollout/epoch structure and GAE charts.
/api/learning-path.done_when: A PPO run beats your best REINFORCE run in wall-clock time.

/api/learning-path.title: Pixels: MinAtar Freeway
/api/learning-path.why: First image-like observations: slower learning, longer runs, real tuning decisions.
/api/learning-path.done_when: Freeway mean reward clearly exceeds the random baseline (~0.5).

/api/learning-path.title: Multi-agent self-play
/api/learning-path.why: Experience action-masked game environments and the self-play adapter.
/api/learning-path.done_when: You understand what experimental means for this pairing.

/api/learning-path.title: Harder control: LunarLander
/api/learning-path.why: Combine everything: shaping rewards, fuel penalties, seed comparisons.

/api/envs/cartpole.name: cartpole
/api/envs/cartpole.label: CartPole-v1
/api/envs/cartpole.description: Balance a pole on a moving cart. The canonical RL starter task: dense rewards, tiny state, fast episodes.
/api/envs/cartpole.termination_desc: Pole falls >12°, cart leaves the track, or 500 steps reached.
limitations: Fully observable; no partial observability challenges.
/api/envs/cartpole.beginner_exercise: Train DQN with default settings for 300-400 episodes. Watch the mean100 curve climb toward 500 - that is 'solved'.
/api/envs/cartpole.advanced_exercise: Compare DQN vs PPO over 5 seeds each. Which is more stable? Measure wall-clock time to reach mean100 ≥ 475.

# RL Testbed experiment file.
# Validate: rltestbed run classic.yaml --dry-run    Launch: rltestbed run classic.yaml
# Or paste it into the Experiments page of the web app.
version: 1
name: Classic Control curriculum
description: Every step of the Classic Control lab curriculum, one seed each.
runs:
