summary.name: Foundations curriculum
summary.description: Every step of the Foundations lab curriculum, one seed each.

modules.title: First contact
modules.summary: What an agent, an episode and a learning curve are, and what learning looks like.

steps.title: Measure the floor
steps.summary: Before training anything, see what no skill looks like.
steps.watch: Episode length jumps around and often hits the 200-step limit; return is mostly the small per-step penalty piling up.
steps.question: Why is a random agent's return in Gridworld negative rather than zero?
steps.answer: Every step costs a little, and a random walk takes many steps to stumble on the goal, so the penalties add up before the episode ends.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Measure the floor
version: 1
name: Measure the floor
description: Before training anything, see what no skill looks like.
runs:
- agent: random
  env: gridworld
  episodes: 50
  seeds:
  - 0

steps.title: Watch values spread
steps.summary: Tabular Q-learning on the same world, three seeds.
steps.watch: Episode length falls from about 50 toward the optimal 10 steps, and the greedy evaluations reach the best return well before training returns do.
steps.question: Why do greedy evaluations look better than the training curve?
steps.answer: Training episodes still explore (ε-greedy), so they include deliberate random moves; evaluations act greedily on what has been learned.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Watch values spread
version: 1
name: Watch values spread
description: Tabular Q-learning on the same world, three seeds.
runs:
- agent: q_learning
  env: gridworld
  episodes: 300
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  - 2

modules.title: Exploration
modules.summary: How to choose between what you know and what you could learn, isolated in bandits.

steps.title: Directed versus random exploration
steps.summary: UCB against ε-greedy sample averages on a 10-armed bandit.
steps.watch: Compare the mean-return curves with ±1σ bands: UCB tends to climb faster and keep rising while ε-greedy flattens.
steps.question: ε-greedy keeps exploring at rate ε forever. What does that cost on a stationary bandit?
steps.answer: Once the best arm is known, every exploratory pull is a guaranteed loss, so regret keeps growing linearly; UCB's bonus shrinks with evidence.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Directed versus random exploration
version: 1
name: Directed versus random exploration
description: UCB against ε-greedy sample averages on a 10-armed bandit.
runs:
- agent: ucb
  env: multi_armed_bandit
  episodes: 1000
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  - 2
  name: UCB
- agent: q_learning
  env: multi_armed_bandit
  episodes: 1000
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  - 2
  name: epsilon-greedy
  params:
    gamma: 0.0
    alpha: 0.1

steps.title: When the world changes
steps.summary: Sample averages versus a constant step size on a drifting bandit.
steps.watch: The constant step size keeps up with the drift; sample averages fall behind as old pulls dominate their estimates.
steps.question: Why does averaging all past rewards fail here?
steps.answer: The true arm values drift, so old rewards describe a world that no longer exists; a constant step size weights recent rewards more.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: When the world changes
version: 1
name: When the world changes
description: Sample averages versus a constant step size on a drifting bandit.
runs:
- agent: ucb
  env: nonstationary_bandit
  episodes: 2000
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  - 2
  name: UCB, sample averages
- agent: ucb
  env: nonstationary_bandit
  episodes: 2000
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  - 2
  name: UCB, step size 0.1
  params:
    alpha: 0.1

modules.title: Learning to act
modules.summary: On-policy versus off-policy learning, and planning with a model.

steps.title: SARSA versus Q-learning on the cliff
steps.summary: The classic on-policy/off-policy comparison.
steps.watch: Training return: SARSA is higher. Greedy evaluation: Q-learning reaches the optimal -13 while SARSA settles on a longer, safer path.
steps.question: Q-learning learns the best path, yet earns less while training. Why?
steps.answer: It learns the value of the greedy policy, which walks the cliff edge, but it acts ε-greedily, so random steps there sometimes fall off. SARSA learns the value of the policy it actually follows, and so avoids the edge.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: SARSA versus Q-learning on the cliff
version: 1
name: SARSA versus Q-learning on the cliff
description: The classic on-policy/off-policy comparison.
runs:
- agent: sarsa
  env: cliff_walking
  episodes: 400
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  - 2
  name: SARSA
- agent: q_learning
  env: cliff_walking
  episodes: 400
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  - 2
  name: Q-learning

steps.title: Plan with a model
steps.summary: Dyna-Q with planning against plain Q-learning on the Dyna maze.
steps.watch: Steps per episode: Dyna-Q drops to about 14 within a few episodes; Q-learning needs many more.
steps.question: Both agents receive exactly the same real experience. Where does Dyna-Q's advantage come from?
steps.answer: Each real step is replayed in imagination many times through the learned model, so the single reward at the goal propagates back through the maze far faster than one update per real step allows.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Plan with a model
version: 1
name: Plan with a model
description: Dyna-Q with planning against plain Q-learning on the Dyna maze.
runs:
- agent: dyna_q
  env: dyna_maze
  episodes: 50
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  - 2
  name: Dyna-Q (10 planning steps)
- agent: q_learning
  env: dyna_maze
  episodes: 50
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  - 2
  name: Q-learning

modules.title: Deep value-based RL
modules.summary: From tables to networks: DQN and the tricks that make it stable.

steps.title: Check the machinery first
steps.summary: DQN on a two-step probe with a delayed reward.
steps.watch: Greedy evaluation should reach 1.0: the agent must value a first step that pays nothing because of what it leads to.
steps.question: Why test on a two-state toy before CartPole?
steps.answer: It has a known answer and trains in seconds. If DQN fails here the cause is a bug or a setting, not the difficulty of the task.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Check the machinery first
version: 1
name: Check the machinery first
description: DQN on a two-step probe with a delayed reward.
runs:
- agent: dqn
  env: probe3
  episodes: 300
  seeds:
  - 0
  params:
    target_update_freq: 20

steps.title: DQN balances a pole
steps.summary: The canonical first deep-RL result, over three seeds.
steps.watch: Greedy evaluations climb toward the solved line at 475 well before the noisy training curve does, and seeds differ a lot.
steps.question: Why does DQN need a replay buffer when tabular Q-learning did not?
steps.answer: Consecutive steps are strongly correlated, and a network trained on them in order overfits to the latest experience. Sampling old transitions at random decorrelates updates and reuses data.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: DQN balances a pole
version: 1
name: DQN balances a pole
description: The canonical first deep-RL result, over three seeds.
runs:
- agent: dqn
  env: cartpole
  episodes: 300
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  - 2

steps.title: How sensitive is it?
steps.summary: A learning-rate sweep for DQN on CartPole.
steps.watch: On the sweep page, check the effect panel for lr and whether the ranking is clear or the seeds overlap.
steps.question: With two seeds per setting, how confident can you be in the winner?
steps.answer: Not very, unless the gap is much larger than the spread between seeds. Rerun the top two settings with more seeds before concluding.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: How sensitive is it?
version: 1
name: How sensitive is it?
description: A learning-rate sweep for DQN on CartPole.
sweeps:
- name: DQN learning rate
  agent: dqn
  env: cartpole
  episodes: 300
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  strategy: grid
  space:
    lr:
      values:
      - 0.0001
      - 0.0005
      - 0.002

steps.title: Fixing overestimation
steps.summary: DQN, Double DQN and Dueling DQN on CartPole.
steps.watch: Differences on CartPole are often within the seed bands. That is itself the lesson: improvements shown on hard benchmarks need not show on easy ones.
steps.question: Why would taking a max over noisy estimates bias them upward?
steps.answer: The max picks whichever estimate happens to be most over-estimated, so its expected value exceeds the true maximum. Double DQN evaluates the chosen action with a different network to break that link.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Fixing overestimation
version: 1
name: Fixing overestimation
description: DQN, Double DQN and Dueling DQN on CartPole.
runs:
- agent: dqn
  env: cartpole
  episodes: 300
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: DQN
- agent: dqn_double
  env: cartpole
  episodes: 300
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: Double DQN
- agent: dueling_dqn
  env: cartpole
  episodes: 300
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: Dueling DQN

modules.title: Policy gradients
modules.summary: Learning the policy directly, and the variance problem that shapes every method.

steps.title: Taming variance with a baseline
steps.summary: REINFORCE with and without a learned baseline.
steps.watch: Compare the width of the ±1σ bands as much as the means.
steps.question: Subtracting a baseline changes every update. Why does it not bias the gradient?
steps.answer: The baseline does not depend on the action, and the expected gradient of log π over actions is zero, so the subtracted term averages out. Only the variance changes.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Taming variance with a baseline
version: 1
name: Taming variance with a baseline
description: REINFORCE with and without a learned baseline.
runs:
- agent: reinforce
  env: cartpole
  episodes: 500
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  - 2
  name: REINFORCE
- agent: reinforce_baseline
  env: cartpole
  episodes: 500
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  - 2
  name: REINFORCE + baseline

steps.title: Actor-critic and trust regions
steps.summary: A2C against PPO on CartPole.
steps.watch: On a PPO run, open the metrics: entropy should fall gently and approx_kl stay small. Spikes in KL often precede collapses.
steps.question: What would happen to PPO without clipping, running ten epochs on each rollout?
steps.answer: It would keep pushing the policy in directions that looked good on stale data, often far beyond where the advantage estimates are valid, and performance can collapse. Clipping removes the incentive past 1 ± ε.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Actor-critic and trust regions
version: 1
name: Actor-critic and trust regions
description: A2C against PPO on CartPole.
runs:
- agent: a2c
  env: cartpole
  episodes: 300
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  - 2
  name: A2C
- agent: ppo
  env: cartpole
  episodes: 300
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  - 2
  name: PPO
  params:
    rollout_steps: 512

modules.title: Continuous control
modules.summary: Actions as vectors of torques instead of buttons.

steps.title: Swing up a pendulum
steps.summary: SAC and TD3 on Pendulum, the smallest continuous task.
steps.watch: Returns start near -1200 (flailing) and should rise toward -200 as the pendulum learns to swing up and balance. Watch SAC's alpha shrink.
steps.question: TD3's actor is deterministic. How does it explore?
steps.answer: By adding noise to its actions during training only; evaluation uses the noiseless action. SAC instead explores through its stochastic policy and the entropy bonus.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Swing up a pendulum
version: 1
name: Swing up a pendulum
description: SAC and TD3 on Pendulum, the smallest continuous task.
runs:
- agent: sac
  env: pendulum
  episodes: 100
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: SAC
- agent: td3
  env: pendulum
  episodes: 100
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: TD3

steps.title: Stability without target networks
steps.summary: SAC against CrossQ on Pendulum.
steps.watch: Both should reach about -150 within 40 episodes. Compare how early each starts improving, and the time per episode: CrossQ's critics are wider.
steps.question: A target network makes learning stable by lagging behind. How does CrossQ stay stable without one?
steps.answer: It batch-normalises its critics and passes current and next state-action pairs through them in one batch, so both halves of the TD target are normalised by the same statistics and stay consistent as the critic changes.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Stability without target networks
version: 1
name: Stability without target networks
description: SAC against CrossQ on Pendulum.
runs:
- agent: sac
  env: pendulum
  episodes: 40
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: SAC
- agent: crossq
  env: pendulum
  episodes: 40
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: CrossQ

steps.title: A simulated body
steps.summary: SAC on MuJoCo's inverted pendulum. Needs the MuJoCo extra.
steps.watch: Watch it in Visualize afterwards: the observation panel names every joint.
steps.question: Why normalise observations for MuJoCo but not for Gridworld?
steps.answer: MuJoCo observations mix quantities on very different scales (angles near 1, velocities near 10). Gridworld's one-hot input is already on one scale.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: A simulated body
version: 1
name: A simulated body
description: SAC on MuJoCo's inverted pendulum. Needs the MuJoCo extra.
runs:
- agent: sac
  env: inverted_pendulum
  episodes: 100
  seeds:
  - 0

modules.title: World models
modules.summary: Learn how the world works, then plan or practise inside the model.

steps.title: Plan with a learned model
steps.summary: PETS against SAC on Pendulum, with the same small budget of episodes.
steps.watch: PETS swings the pendulum up within about five episodes; SAC is still learning at twelve. Compare wall-clock time too: PETS plans at every step.
steps.question: PETS never trains a policy. How does it choose actions?
steps.answer: At every step it imagines hundreds of action sequences in its learned model, scores each by imagined return, refines them with the cross-entropy method, executes the first action of the best one, and then plans again.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Plan with a learned model
version: 1
name: Plan with a learned model
description: PETS against SAC on Pendulum, with the same small budget of episodes.
runs:
- agent: pets
  env: pendulum
  episodes: 12
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: PETS
- agent: sac
  env: pendulum
  episodes: 12
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: SAC

steps.title: Where imagination breaks
steps.summary: PETS on CartPole; open the Imagination tab of the run.
steps.watch: Compare model_error_1 with model_error_15 in the metric charts, then look at how the imagined trajectory leaves the real one after a few steps.
steps.question: The model is nearly exact one step ahead. Why does it drift over fifteen?
steps.answer: Each prediction becomes the input to the next, so small errors are fed back and grow, often into states the model never saw in training. Short horizons and replanning every step keep this under control.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Where imagination breaks
version: 1
name: Where imagination breaks
description: PETS on CartPole; open the Imagination tab of the run.
runs:
- agent: pets
  env: cartpole
  episodes: 10
  seeds:
  - 0

steps.title: Learning in imagination
steps.summary: Dreamer-lite trains a policy inside the model; compare it with planning.
steps.watch: Both learn within a handful of episodes. Dreamer-lite acts with one network pass per step; PETS plans every step. Its imagined_return metric shows what the policy expects; compare it with real returns.
steps.question: Why would imagined returns be higher than real ones?
steps.answer: The actor is optimised against the model, so it seeks out actions where the model is too optimistic. Errors in the world model become errors in the policy, which is why imagined rollouts are kept short.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Learning in imagination
version: 1
name: Learning in imagination
description: Dreamer-lite trains a policy inside the model; compare it with planning.
runs:
- agent: dreamer_lite
  env: pendulum
  episodes: 20
  seeds:
  - 0
  name: Dreamer-lite
- agent: pets
  env: pendulum
  episodes: 20
  seeds:
  - 0
  name: PETS

modules.title: RL for language models
modules.summary: The methods behind reasoning models, on a tiny transformer: verifiers, groups, KL and preferences.

steps.title: Sharpen a model with a verifier
steps.summary: GRPO and REINFORCE fine-tune a pretrained model on addition, scored right or wrong.
steps.watch: Sampled accuracy rises from about 0.5 toward 0.9 while entropy falls and KL to the base model grows. Open the Samples tab of a run to read its answers.
steps.question: The base model's greedy answer is already right almost every time. What is RL improving?
steps.answer: The sampling distribution: a single sample at temperature 1 is right only about half the time. RL moves probability onto the correct answer, so samples agree with the greedy answer. This sharpening is most of what RL with verifiable rewards does.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Sharpen a model with a verifier
version: 1
name: Sharpen a model with a verifier
description: GRPO and REINFORCE fine-tune a pretrained model on addition, scored right or wrong.
runs:
- agent: grpo
  env: lm_addition
  episodes: 60
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: GRPO
- agent: lm_reinforce
  env: lm_addition
  episodes: 60
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: REINFORCE

steps.title: Reward hacking and the KL anchor
steps.summary: A flawed reward model pays for length. Compare no KL penalty with a strong one.
steps.watch: Switch the comparison metric between reward and accuracy. Without KL, reward climbs to its maximum of 2.0 while accuracy falls to zero; with KL 0.5, reward rises less and accuracy rises.
steps.question: Reward went up and the model got worse. How would you notice this if you only had the reward?
steps.answer: You could not, from the reward alone. You need a second measurement the policy is not optimising (here, accuracy), samples you read yourself, or a KL budget that flags runaway drift. Measuring only the optimised quantity hides reward hacking.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Reward hacking and the KL anchor
version: 1
name: Reward hacking and the KL anchor
description: A flawed reward model pays for length. Compare no KL penalty with a strong one.
runs:
- agent: grpo
  env: lm_addition_hackable
  episodes: 80
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: GRPO, no KL
  params:
    kl_coef: 0.0
- agent: grpo
  env: lm_addition_hackable
  episodes: 80
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: GRPO, KL 0.5
  params:
    kl_coef: 0.5

steps.title: Refining GRPO: DAPO
steps.summary: GRPO against its DAPO variant on addition.
steps.watch: DAPO tends to be ahead early (dynamic sampling means every update carries signal) and needs extra sampling rounds to do it. Compare the entropy charts: here they fall about equally.
steps.question: Clip-higher exists to stop entropy collapsing. Why is the effect hard to see in this lab?
steps.answer: Collapse becomes a problem over long training on hard problems, where the policy must keep exploring for many steps. These tasks are learned in a few dozen steps and the right answer is already likely, so there is little exploration left to protect. Results at small scale do not always transfer.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Refining GRPO: DAPO
version: 1
name: 'Refining GRPO: DAPO'
description: GRPO against its DAPO variant on addition.
runs:
- agent: grpo
  env: lm_addition
  episodes: 60
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: GRPO
- agent: grpo
  env: lm_addition
  episodes: 60
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: DAPO
  params:
    clip_eps_high: 0.28
    dynamic_sampling: true
    token_level_loss: true
    kl_coef: 0.0

steps.title: Preferences instead of rewards
steps.summary: DPO learns from which of two answers is better; GRPO from verified scores.
steps.watch: DPO improves less than GRPO here: its pairs come from the fixed base model, so they stop being informative as the policy moves. Try the online-pairs option.
steps.question: DPO never computes a reward during training. Where does the information come from?
steps.answer: From the preference labels on each pair: which answer is better. DPO turns the KL-regularised RL objective into a classification loss on those pairs, measured relative to the reference model.
steps.experiment_text:
# Learning path step: Preferences instead of rewards
version: 1
name: Preferences instead of rewards
description: DPO learns from which of two answers is better; GRPO from verified scores.
runs:
- agent: dpo
  env: lm_sort
  episodes: 60
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: DPO
- agent: grpo
  env: lm_sort
  episodes: 60
  seeds:
  - 0
  - 1
  name: GRPO
